title: Zan
recipe: Cook finger millet flour with water into a thick porridge, adding chopped Jain-friendly seasonal vegetables.
Season lightly with salt. Serve hot.
tips: Millet-based and highly nutritious – rich in fibre, calcium and iron.
Can be paired with a Jain-friendly chilli chutney.

title: Thukpa

ingredients.name: Chicken, pork or other local meat

recipe: Prepare a light broth with meat, ginger, garlic, local herbs and chilli.
Add noodles and cook until soft. Serve hot.
tips: This version is specifically prepared with meat.
Vegetarian Thukpa can be represented as a separate recipe if needed.

title: Steamed Rice with Boiled Vegetables
recipe: Steam or boil rice. Separately boil seasonal greens and vegetables with minimal seasoning.
Serve together as a simple, everyday start to the day.
tips: Rice is the absolute staple across almost all tribes.
Often accompanied by a fermented side or chilli.

title: Pika Pila

ingredients.name: Pork fat, local chilli (including king chilli), salt

recipe: Combine fermented bamboo shoot with pork fat and crushed local chillies.
Mix well into a tangy, spicy, pungent condiment or side.
Serve with rice.
tips: The fermentation of bamboo shoot gives deep aroma and tang.
Extremely flavourful and polarising for newcomers.

title: Pork with Bamboo Shoot
recipe: Cook pork with ginger and chilli until tender. Add bamboo shoot and continue simmering until flavours meld.
Serve with steamed rice.
tips: Bamboo shoot (fresh, dried or fermented) is used extensively throughout the state.
Minimal spices let the ingredients shine.

title: Chura Sabzi

ingredients.name: Jain-friendly seasonal vegetables, chilli flakes, salt

recipe: Cook Jain-friendly seasonal vegetables with pieces of fermented cheese (churpi/chura) and chilli.
Simmer until the cheese softens and flavours the vegetables.
Serve with rice.
tips: Fermented yak or cow cheese adds a unique creamy, tangy depth.
Use only Jain-friendly vegetables for the Jain-friendly version.

title: Lukter

ingredients.name: Sun-dried or smoked meat (beef, pork or mithun)

recipe: Shred or chop the dried/smoked meat and toss with crushed dry chilli and salt.
Serve as a spicy, high-protein side or snack with rice.
tips: Preserved meat preparation – ideal for long storage in the hills.
Very spicy and flavourful.

title: Pasa (Fish Soup)
recipe: Prepare a light, clear broth with fish, ginger, local herbs and chilli.
Simmer until the fish is cooked. Serve hot with rice.
tips: Simple fish soup common in many communities.
Can use river fish or smoked varieties.

title: Millet / Buckwheat Momo

ingredients.name: Millet or buckwheat flour for wrapper

recipe: Make dough from millet or buckwheat flour. Prepare a filling of local greens or cheese.
Shape into momos and steam until cooked.
Serve with chilli sauce.
tips: Traditional versions use local grains rather than refined flour.
Potato-filled versions are not considered Jain-friendly, so the Jain status here applies to the greens or cheese filling.

title: Apong (Rice Beer)
recipe: Cook rice or millet, cool, mix with traditional starter culture, and ferment for several days.
Strain and serve the mildly alcoholic, earthy rice beer in bamboo mugs.
Traditionally served at social gatherings and festivals across many tribes.
tips: Apong (or Apo) is a traditional fermented alcoholic beverage of Arunachal Pradesh.
Strength and flavour vary by tribe and preparation.
Classified as a beverage rather than a food or snack.

title: Boiled Local Greens

ingredients.name: Jain-friendly leafy greens and non-root wild herbs

recipe: Boil or steam the Jain-friendly greens with ginger and a little chilli until tender.
Season with salt. Serve as a simple, nutritious side with rice.
tips: Wild and cultivated greens form a major part of the diet.
The Jain-friendly version excludes onion, garlic and root vegetables.

title: Mithun / Pork Stew
recipe: Slow-cook the meat with ginger, local herbs and chilli until very tender.
Keep the gravy light. Serve with rice.
tips: Mithun is considered sacred and a status symbol among many tribes.
Simple boiling or stewing is the traditional method.
